agent_7.question: The policy doesn’t specify what happens if a fisher fails to deposit the required 7 kg per trip—who monitors compliance and what is the consequence?
agent_7.answer:
The committee will do the check. Every fisher brings his catch to the dock and the rotating committee records the 8‑kg haul. They will count the 1‑kg that the fisher keeps and confirm that the remaining 7 kg is deposited into the reserve. If a fisher turns up without depositing the 7 kg, he must pay a penalty equal to that missing amount – the fish or equivalent value – into the reserve. If the same fisher fails to deposit more than twice in a month, he will be barred from fishing for one round until he clears his debt. That way the reserve stays stocked and everyone keeps to the rule, but we still get the fish we need to survive.

Policy

Each fisher may take up to 8 kg per trip, must keep 1 kg for personal survival, deposit the other 7 kg into the community reserve; fishing is suspended when the lake stock falls below 45 kg and resumes when it rises above 60 kg. Compliance: the rotating committee will verify deposits at the dock. If a fisher fails to deposit, he must pay a penalty equal to the missing amount to the reserve. Repeated non‑compliance (more than two times in a month) results in a one‑round fishing ban.

Operationalization

After each trip, the fisher returns to the dock and presents his catch to the rotating committee. The committee records the 1 kg kept and verifies that the remaining 7 kg is deposited into the community reserve. If a fisher does not deposit, the committee notes the shortfall and requires payment of the missing amount into the reserve. Penalties are added to the reserve. Failing to comply more than twice in a month triggers a one‑round ban, after which the fisher must clear any outstanding debt before fishing again.

agent_7.answer: We keep a simple gauge at the dock that everyone can read before leaving. Every fisher has to check it before each trip and shout out the reading. If someone goes out when the gauge is low, they’re fined for the missing deposit and, after two such offenses in a month, banned for one round. That way the lake’s level is checked daily by the crew, and the policy is enforced even though the committee only formally reviews the gauge monthly.

agent_9.question: The proposal doesn't specify how each fisher’s reserve is tracked or who has authority over it.
agent_9.answer: Hey community, we keep each fisher’s reserve on the shared ledger that everyone updates after every trip. Every fisher writes down the total catch, how much they keep (max 8 kg including the 1 kg survival), and how much is deposited into the reserve. The ledger is maintained by the community steward, a role we rotate each month. The steward makes sure the numbers add up, but no one has exclusive control; all fishers can see the ledger and ask questions. The reserve can only be used by fishers whose personal reserve has been below 1 kg for the last two trips, and withdrawals are capped at 2 kg per trip. All decisions about the reserve—like changes in limits—are made at our monthly meetings by a simple majority vote. That way everyone knows their own balance and who is overseeing the reserve.

That means if you pull 9 kg, the 1 kg over the 8 kg cap is logged as excess, and 0.1 kg of your reserve is taken as a fee. If the excess is larger, the fee scales proportionally. The same rule applies if you fail to deposit the excess – the excess is first added to the communal reserve and then 10 % of that amount is removed from your reserve.

agent_0.question: What defines a cycle, and how is a fisher’s ban for one cycle enforced and tracked?
agent_0.answer:
In our community a cycle is the time span between two consecutive fishing rounds – that is, one round of fishing plus the meeting where we record the catch and vote on the next rules.  A fisher who breaches the limit or fails to deposit is automatically barred for the next round, so the ban lasts exactly one cycle.  The ban is tracked and enforced by the communal ledger and the community council.  At the start of every round the council reads the ledger; any name flagged as "banned until cycle X" is not allowed to register a new haul.  If a banned fisher attempts to fish, the crew will refuse to let him take a hook and will return any fish he has caught.  The ban flag is cleared automatically in the ledger once the cycle in which it was imposed has passed – the next community meeting updates the record and removes the ban.

Thus a cycle is simply one round of fishing, and the ban is enforced by a community‑maintained ledger that lists the fisher’s status and is consulted before each trip.

agent_1.question: Who serves as the rotating monitor and how is the rotation decided?
agent_1.answer: The rotating monitor will be chosen by a simple draw among all active fishers at the start of each month. Each fisher puts their name in a hat, and a neutral facilitator—usually the community elder or a respected non‑fishing resident—draws a name. The fisher whose name is drawn will serve as monitor for the following month, stepping aside when they fish themselves. The monitor’s role is purely observational: they tally catches, check that no one exceeds the 2 % trip limit or the 6 % weekly cap, and verify the reserve never falls below 25 %. They must not catch fish during the month they are monitoring to avoid a conflict of interest. If a fisher is absent for the month, the next drawn name will fill the spot. This simple rotation keeps the process fair and transparent.

agent_1.answer: In our community we decide the fine by looking at how far a fisher went over the limit and taking a set percentage of that excess.  We usually use 10 % of the amount that exceeds the 2 % cap.  The fisherman who caught too much must report the catch to the council at the next meeting, prove the excess, and then the council agrees on the fine amount.  The fine is due within seven days and is paid into the communal sustainability fund that we use to keep the lake healthy and repair gear.  This way the cost of over‑catch is borne by the offender but also strengthens the lake for everyone.

agent_1.answer: As the community treasurer, I will be the one who collects fine payments. The ledger is kept in a shared ledger book that everyone can see at the weekly meeting and is also updated in a digital file that the council can audit quarterly. If a fisher does not submit payment within the seven‑day deadline, I will issue the second fine (15 % of the outstanding amount) and update the ledger entry to reflect the new fine amount and the pending status. The fisher will be notified in writing that their fishing rights may be suspended temporarily until the fine is cleared. agent_5.question: Who appoints the scribe, how is that person selected, and what authority does the scribe hold to enforce the rules?
agent_5.answer: The scribe is chosen by the whole community – we vote for one person each round who is trusted, fair, and has no stake in a particular catch. The scribe’s authority comes from that collective vote: they may record the pre‑trip lake stock, log each fisher’s haul, check that no one exceeded 12 kg and that at least 25 % of the pre‑trip stock remains, return any excess to the lake, impose the one‑round ban and 10 % fine, and must keep accurate records that the community can audit. The scribe is accountable to the community and can be replaced by a new vote if the community feels the scribe is not acting fairly.

That reserve is kept in a communal cellar under the scribe’s supervision and is used for community meals, to feed members who need extra food, or traded for goods and services as the community decides. In short, the fine is a fish penalty that the community collects, holds, and allocates as a shared resource.

agent_8.answer: In this game a "round" is the collective fishing cycle that starts when the first fisher begins a trip after the previous round has finished and ends either when every fisher has taken their turn for that cycle or when the cumulative catch would push the community’s total above the 25 % ceiling. We normally give each fisher one trip per round – that keeps the lake’s regeneration rate in mind. The chair checks each trip against the 12 % of the lake’s current volume. The round’s end is simply when the chair has recorded the last fisher’s trip for that cycle – no more fish are taken in that round until the lake’s volume has been replenished enough that another round can begin. agent_9.question: Who is responsible for holding and managing the communal reserve box?
agent_9.answer: The keeper, the elder we trust, is responsible for holding and managing the communal reserve box. He/she keeps it in a secure place at the communal area, logs each transfer, and releases fish only when a fisher meets the withdrawal criteria.
agent_9.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 6 kg per trip, must keep 1 kg for personal survival; any fish beyond 6 kg is deposited into a communal reserve, and fishers whose reserves have been below 1 kg for two consecutive trips may withdraw up to 2 kg per trip from that reserve.
agent_9.revised_operationalization: Every trip, a fisher records the weight taken and the weight kept. The keeper verifies the records. If a fisher fails to keep 1 kg or deposit excess, that fisher's entire catch that trip is forfeited, and on the next trip the fisher must return 2 kg to the lake or deposit it to reserve. Violations are noted on the community ledger and, if repeated, result in a temporary fishing ban for one week.
